title: How a law practice should write an about page
metaTitle: Law practice about page: name the people
excerpt: A law practice about page should name who does the work and why that matters to this client. Keep the origin story only if it changes the ask.
alt: A white modernist building with stacked cubic volumes and tall windows against a pale sky, architecture as identity in the way an about page should name people.
caption: A building that is recognizable because of its shape, not because of a motto. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs at the top of a law firm about page?
faqs.answer: Put the people who do the work first, with the matters they handle. A client choosing counsel under time pressure needs a name and a fit, not a founding year. Move the firm history below that, unless the history itself states a boundary the client must know.

faqs.question: How long should a lawyer's biography be?
faqs.answer: Four to six specific sentences are enough. Cover the role, the matters, the boundary, how they work, and where they are admitted. A list of every file they have touched hides the work you want to be hired for.

faqs.question: Should the about page include an origin story?
faqs.answer: Include it when the story changes whether this client should request a consultation. A practice that acts only for tenants can say so up front. A tale about a pen, a motto, or the year you opened can sit lower, or leave the page.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A law practice about page is proof that people stand behind the offer. Name who does the work, and say why a client choosing counsel under time pressure should care. Skip the origin myth unless that story changes the decision to request a consultation.

Google's helpful-content guidance treats "who" as part of trust. It asks whether a visitor can tell who created the page, and it gives more weight to experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trust on topics that can affect safety, health, or financial stability. Choosing a lawyer is that kind of topic. A marble building and a founding year do not answer who will read the lease.

## People are the proof

The client has already seen the matter, or they are about to. The about page answers a different question. Who will sit with this problem, and why is that person a fit for this kind of matter?

Lead with the lawyers who take the work, not with a group photograph and a century of adjectives. For each person, a reader should get the name, the role, the matters they actually handle, and the jurisdictions where they can act. Those four facts are the proof. Charm is optional.

If a coordinator, a clerk, or a paralegal is who replies first, name them too, and say what they do. A client under time pressure is calmed by knowing the path, including the person who is not the partner. Hiding the team makes the firm look like a single invisible expert.

Google also warns against vague titles such as "Profile" when the page is about a specific person. Give each person a heading that includes their name and the work they do. "Amira Shah, shop leases and commercial contracts" is a title a client can use. "Our team" is a label that still needs a click.

## Why this client should care

The reason to care is the overlap between their matter and this person's work. Write that overlap in one or two sentences. "She reviews leases for independent shops and will tell you before you sign if the guarantee is broader than the shop." That sentence helps a tenant. A paragraph about loving the law since childhood does not.

Keep the reason tied to the kind of matter you take. If the practice is employment advice for small companies, say the kinds of letters and decisions that person handles. If you want the client to request a consultation, the biography should make that request feel specific. "Write to her about a termination letter" is a next step. "She is passionate about justice" is a mood.

Add the practical facts that change a booking. Languages they can work in. Cities where they meet. Days they are in the office, if that is stable. Whether they supervise the work or do it themselves. A founder hiring counsel for a company, or a shop owner hiring for a lease, is allowed to care who drafts the document.

Leave rankings and awards in a quiet list, and only when they are real and current. They are not a substitute for the sentence about the work. A badge beside an empty bio is the same costume as a Latin motto.

Admission and insurance details belong here when a client would be right to ask. Name the roll or the bar, in the words your regulator uses, and name the state or country. If you carry professional indemnity insurance and you are expected to say so, say so in one line. A client under time pressure should not have to open a PDF in the footer to learn whether you can act for them where they live.

## The origin myth test

Most firm histories fail a simple test. If you delete the story and the client would still know whether to request a consultation, the story can wait, or leave the site.

"We opened in 1994 after two partners left a larger firm" rarely changes a lease decision this week. Keep it if a referring lawyer expects it, and put it below the people. Do not let it be the first screen of the about page.

The story earns its place when it changes the fit. A practice that exists because the founders were shop tenants, and that still only acts for tenants, is a boundary. A practice that started inside a union, and still acts for workers rather than employers, is a boundary. Write the constraint, then the date. The date is the less important half.

A long narrative about a grandfather's pen, a trip, or a motto translated from Latin reassures the people who lived it. The client with a deadline did not. Nielsen Norman Group's finding that people read only about a quarter of the text on pages they visit is a reason to spend that quarter on names and matters.

## What a short biography can hold

Four to six sentences are enough for a person when the sentences are specific.

Name and role. The matters they take, in client language. The boundary, including work they do not do. One concrete detail of how they work, such as marking up the document itself rather than sending a separate essay. Where they are admitted to practice. How to request a consultation with them, if clients can ask for a person.

Avoid a list of every matter they have ever touched. It recreates the vague grid on a different page. Match the biography to the services you feature. If the services page says you review shop leases, the about page should show the person who does that review.

Write in the third person if several people share the page, and keep the tone even. Superlatives about being the leading lawyer in the city are hard to trust and easy to regret. A specific description of the work is stronger, and it is easier to keep true.

If a person has left, take them off the page the week they leave. An about page that still offers a consultation with someone who is gone is a trust failure, and on a legal site it is also a practical one. The client may write to a dead address on the worst day of their month.

## Photographs should identify, not decorate

Use a photograph in which the person is recognizable, taken in the room where they actually work if you can. A client who has a video call later should be able to tell they reached the right human. Marble, a column, and a borrowed courthouse do not identify anyone.

Match the picture to the sentence. If the bio says she reviews leases, a photo of her at a table with paper is enough. A photo of a skyline identifies the city, maybe, and it does not identify counsel.

Write alt text that describes the person and the setting. "Amira Shah at a wooden table with a marked-up lease" is useful. "Excellence" is not a description of a photograph. Captions can carry the matter line in plain language.

If someone does not want their face published, use their name and work anyway, and say that meetings are by video or in the office. Absence of a photo is honest. A stock face is not.

## How the page ends

Close on the consultation, with a sentence about what happens next. The client has just read who does the work. Let them ask for that person, or for the matter, without hunting through the footer.

Say what to have ready, in one line. The draft, the deadline, the other party's name. Repeat that the first reply is about fit, not a legal opinion by email.

Link back to the two or three services those people actually deliver, so the about page and the services page agree. A bio that promises employment trials, while the services page only offers letter advice, is a contradiction a careful client will notice.

Read the page as if you had ten seconds. Who works here, and what do they take? If the answer is a founding year, rewrite the opening. Jakob Nielsen's rule from the Nielsen Norman Group research is that value has to be clear within 10 seconds if you want someone to stay for minutes. On this page the value is a person matched to a matter.

## When a story is the right first screen

Keep the origin at the top only when it is the boundary. "We act for tenants, not landlords" can be the first sentence if it is true and if it is the reason the firm exists. Follow it immediately with the people who do that work today. A story about the past, with the current lawyers postponed, asks the client to care about you before they know you can help.

The next page they need, once they trust a person, is evidence of how a matter was handled. A face is not a case. Read [how a proof page shows the decision](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-law-practice) before you publish a result you are not allowed to show.

When you want to see how other studios put real work next to real names, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The standard is the same. Specific, and something a stranger can check.
